title: "Using your own data"
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8,
                      fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 96, message = FALSE,
                      warning = FALSE)
```

## The input format

factomics needs **a named list of numeric matrices, one per omics layer, with
features in rows and samples in columns**. Column names are sample IDs and must
be the same set in every matrix (the order may differ; factomics aligns them).
Row names are feature IDs.

```
X <- list(
  transcriptome = <genes x samples matrix>,
  metabolome    = <metabolites x samples matrix>,
  microbiome    = <taxa x samples matrix>
)
```

Metadata is a data frame with one row per sample and a column holding the
sample IDs (`"sample"` by default; set `sample_col` otherwise).

## Reading CSV or Excel files

If each file has feature IDs in the first column and one column per sample:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
read_view <- function(path) as.matrix(read.csv(path, row.names = 1,
                                               check.names = FALSE))
X <- list(
  rna = read_view("data/rna_counts_normalised.csv"),
  met = read_view("data/metabolites.csv")
)
meta <- read.csv("data/metadata.csv")
```

For Excel files, `readxl::read_excel()` gives a data frame; move the first
column to the row names before `as.matrix()`:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
read_xlsx_view <- function(path, sheet = 1) {
  df <- as.data.frame(readxl::read_excel(path, sheet = sheet))
  rownames(df) <- df[[1]]
  as.matrix(df[, -1])
}
```

If your files are **samples x features** instead, transpose with `t()`.

## Keeping only shared samples

```{r, eval = FALSE}
common <- Reduce(intersect, lapply(X, colnames))
X <- lapply(X, function(m) m[, common])
```

## Preprocessing advice

factomics z-scores each feature by default (`scale_features = TRUE`). What it
does **not** do is the omics-specific normalisation, which you should apply
first:

| Data type | Typical preparation |
|-----------|---------------------|
| RNA-seq counts | library-size normalisation and a log or variance-stabilising transform (e.g. `DESeq2::vst()`) |
| Microbiome counts | filter rare taxa, then a centred log-ratio (CLR) transform |
| Metabolomics / lipidomics | log transform, impute or drop features with many missing values |
| Methylation | M-values rather than beta values |

Also consider keeping only the most variable features per view (for example the
top 2,000 genes), which speeds every method up and removes noise:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
top_var <- function(m, n) m[order(-apply(m, 1, var))[seq_len(min(n, nrow(m)))], ]
X$rna <- top_var(X$rna, 2000)
```

Missing values are set to zero after scaling (that is, to the feature mean).
MOFA2 can model missing values natively; for the other methods, impute or remove
heavily missing features beforehand.

## A worked example with files

To show the whole route, we write simulated data to CSV files, read them back
and analyse them:

```{r}
library(factomics)
sim <- simulate_multiomics(n_samples = 40, seed = 2)
dir <- tempfile("mydata"); dir.create(dir)
for (v in names(sim$data))
  write.csv(sim$data[[v]], file.path(dir, paste0(v, ".csv")))
write.csv(sim$metadata, file.path(dir, "metadata.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

files <- list.files(dir, pattern = "csv$", full.names = TRUE)
files <- files[basename(files) != "metadata.csv"]
X <- lapply(setNames(files, sub("\\.csv$", "", basename(files))),
            function(f) as.matrix(read.csv(f, row.names = 1,
                                           check.names = FALSE)))
meta <- read.csv(file.path(dir, "metadata.csv"))

fx <- factomics(X, metadata = meta, methods = c("PCA", "MFA", "JIVE"), k = 3,
                embeddings = "umap", verbose = FALSE)
fx
```

```{r, fig.height = 3.4}
plot_embedding(fx$embeddings, meta, color_by = "group")
```

Save everything as CSV tables:

```{r}
out <- export_results(fx, file.path(dir, "results"))
basename(out)
```
